📌 Description

The logits a sparse-attention selector ranks by, over a paged KV cache:

score(row, col) = sum_h max(0, dot(K[col], Q[row, h])) / divisor

There is no softmax and no value aggregation — this is the input to a top-k, not an attention output. Producing it with the existing prefill kernels means materialising an attention output nobody reads.

API and contract

sparse_paged_scores(q, k_cache, page_table, token_to_req, query_positions, sequence_lengths, compress_ratio, divisor, num_columns=None, logits=None, visible_blocks=None)

q is [rows, num_heads, head_dim], float16 or bfloat16, head_dim 64/128/192/256 and at most 16 heads. k_cache is [pages, page_size, head_dim].

A query sees only the compressed entries whose tokens are all behind it. Entries on a page the block table does not map come out as -inf, so a top-k never selects them. Columns past what the query can see are left untouched instead, and the returned count is the number of entries actually scored — what the query can see, capped by the column width — so a top-k bounds itself by that count rather than by the width.

The ReLU applies to a head's completed dot product, so the feature axis is fully accumulated before the heads are summed.

Both staged loads are 128 bits wide. Strides alone do not settle whether every address they form is aligned — a view onto the middle of a tensor keeps its strides and carries a base that is not — so the query includes its base in the test it runs and falls back to an element-wise path, and the cache has a per-element staging path of its own because cp_async has no narrower form.

The kernel needs m16n8k16, so the capability is checked against the device the query is on rather than once against whichever device was current first.

Shape and cache level

A block resolves one cache address per column into shared memory before it stages anything, in the eight bytes a column already spent on the page and the entry, so the staging loop is a shared load and an add per copy rather than a 64-bit page multiply and a divergent branch recomputed by each of the eight threads covering a column. Columns with no page carry the first page's address and a bitmask marks them, so the copy needs no predicate; a cache with no pages at all has no first address to carry, so those launches skip staging outright.

Rows of one request read the same keys and their blocks run together, so the keys are staged with cp.async.ca rather than the cg form that bypasses L1. cp_async gains a CacheMode for this, defaulting to cg so nothing else changes: the SASS of an existing prefill module is identical across the commit that adds it, all 509266 instructions of it.

The launch turns over from one column tile per block to eight at 24 blocks per SM. The single-tile block stages the whole head in one step and has nothing to overlap inside itself, so other blocks on the same SM are what hide its latency and it keeps winning well past a full wave. What it does not scale with is the occupancy: sweeping rows at three shapes, the last block count the single-tile shape wins and the first the eight-tile shape does are 1536 then 2048 at sixteen heads and head dim 128 (7 blocks/SM), 2048 then 4096 at four heads (7 blocks/SM), and 1536 then 2048 at eight heads and head dim 256 (4 blocks/SM). The first and third turn at the same block count with very different occupancy, so a threshold in waves cannot fit them — those windows are (3.1, 4.2], (4.2, 8.4] and (5.5, 7.3] waves, the first two disjoint — while per SM they are (21.9, 29.3], (29.3, 58.5] and (21.9, 29.3], which 24 splits. Four heads at 2048 blocks is the one point that lands on the wrong side, by 1.09x; it and the 2048 of the other two want opposite shapes.

The threshold is measured on SM80 only. It decides which of the two shapes runs, never what either computes, so the worst case elsewhere is a slower choice.

Eight query heads or fewer take mma.m16n8k16 instead of multiplying eight columns of padding, which needs an ldmatrix.x2 the wrapper set did not have. The query fragments are held in registers across the column tiles rather than reloaded per multiply, except at head dim 256 above eight heads, where they do not fit.

Verification

The AOT registration is covered too. The kernel needs m16n8k16, which every SM8-or-newer device has, so the module is registered whenever any target is that new rather than only when an 8.x target is in the build. Restoring the narrower gate fails five of the seven.

Compared against a reference that walks the page table in plain torch and never calls the kernel, across both dtypes, head dimensions 64/128/192/256, one, four, eight, nine and sixteen heads, both launch shapes, a cache with no pages, an unmapped page, a row whose request is invalid, a column width narrower than the query can see, and that a row leaves the columns past its own count as the caller left them. Eight heads and nine straddle the two multiply widths, and sixteen at head dim 256 is the shape that reloads its query fragments.

The launch shapes are pinned against each other as well: enough blocks to fill the device switches from one column tile per block to eight, and scoring the same rows one at a time takes the other shape, so the two are required to agree column for column. Forcing either shape for the whole file passes all 51.

Alignment is pinned in both directions: a query and a cache passed as views with a misaligned base but aligned strides. Removing either base check alone fails its own case with cudaErrorMisalignedAddress, so the tests pin the check rather than the surrounding stride guard.

benchmarks/bench_sparse_paged_scores.py on SM80, median of three runs, microseconds:

rows heads head dim columns us
1 4 128 1024 3.87
1 16 128 4096 3.65
8 16 128 4096 5.63
16 16 128 4096 8.34
40 8 256 2048 14.54
48 8 256 2048 17.12
64 4 128 1024 10.38
64 16 128 4096 17.74
512 8 256 2048 94.61
2048 4 128 1024 92.06
2048 16 128 4096 373.00

Replayed from a graph: the smallest of these is a few microseconds, the same order as a launch, so timing them one launch at a time would measure the launch as much as the kernel. Every run of the eleven lands within 1% of the median except the second, which spans 3.60 to 4.69.

The two single-row shapes are a floor rather than a gap left open. At sixteen to sixty-four blocks the kernel is bound by its prologue -- the request, its length, the visible count, then the page table, then the staging -- and not by the work: more blocks move it nowhere, measured at 32 and at 16 columns per block, and pipelining the single-tile launch's staging makes it slower rather than faster.

Writing the reference turned up a gap that is fixed here: num_columns was ignored whenever logits was supplied, because the kernel takes its width from the tensor it writes. The wrapper now rejects the mismatch.

The kernel here is independent of the route kernels and the pre-indexer alongside this, sharing only an export line and an AOT registration with them, and shares no file at all with the block-sparse wrapper PR. Every merge order of the four was checked to apply cleanly.

🔍 Related Issues

This is one of four independent building blocks for a block-granular sparse-attention
selector. Each stands alone and none depends on another being merged first:

  • a pre-indexer that builds the compressed rows the selector reads
  • a scorer that ranks a paged KV cache against a multi-head query
  • route kernels that turn a block selection into the tokens behind it
  • a block-sparse wrapper path that reads a raw paged cache through that route

Nothing in the repository calls them yet -- the consumer is a model implementation
outside it -- so they are building blocks for a later integration rather than a
finished feature. They share no kernel and no binding; the only files two of them
touch in common are the export list and the AOT registration.

it builds: without it an install with JIT disabled has no artifact to

Profiling put the scorer's cost in three places, none of them the multiply.

Address arithmetic. Staging issued 34 instructions per 16-byte copy: a 64-bit
page multiply, two shared loads and a divergent branch, all recomputed by each
of the eight threads covering a column, in a loop whose trip count was not
constant. The block now resolves one address per column into shared memory
before it stages anything, in the eight bytes a column already spent on the
page and the entry, and the staging loop unrolls to a shared load and an add
per copy. Columns with no page carry the first page's address and a bitmask
marks them, so the copy needs no predicate either. 138M instructions to 65M.
A cache with no pages at all has no first address to carry, so those launches
skip the staging outright.

Cache level. cp.async.cg bypasses L1, and rows of one request read the same
keys, so every repeat was going to L2: 46M sectors for bytes that fit in far
fewer. cp_async gains a CacheMode and the scorer takes cp.async.ca. L1 hit rate
0.7% to 22.5%. The mode defaults to the cg form everywhere else: the SASS of an
existing prefill module is unchanged across this commit, all 509266
instructions of it.

Tile width. Sixteen query heads were multiplied whatever the model has, so a
four-head model spent three quarters of its tensor work on padding. The tile
width is now a template parameter and eight-head shapes take mma.m16n8k16,
which needs an ldmatrix.x2 the wrapper set did not have.

The query fragments are also held in registers across the column tiles rather
than reloaded per multiply, which needs the slice offset to be a constant, so
slices became the inner loop. Head dim 256 at more than eight heads is the one
shape whose fragments do not fit, and it keeps reloading them.
perf(attention): turn the scorer's launch over at four waves, not one
4170db9 
One column tile per block re-stages the query for every tile, so the eight-tile
shape takes over once the device is full. It was taking over after a single
wave of blocks, which is far too early: the single-tile block stages the whole
head in one step and has nothing to overlap inside itself, so what hides its
latency is other blocks on the same SM, and it keeps winning well past one
wave.

Sweeping rows at three shapes on SM80 puts the turn at four. In blocks, the
last count the single-tile shape wins and the first the eight-tile shape does:
1536 then 2048 at sixteen heads and head dim 128, 2048 then 4096 at four heads,
and already lost by 2048 at eight heads and head dim 256. All three report
seven blocks per SM on this part, so one wave is 490 and four is 1960, which
splits every one of those correctly.

Between 8 and 24 rows the old threshold sent every launch to the shape that
loses there. Forcing each shape and comparing, at 4096 columns and sixteen
heads the eight-tile shape costs 1.64x at 8 rows and 1.28x at 16. Everything
outside that range keeps the shape it already picked.

One row is unaffected. With sixteen to sixty-four blocks the kernel is bound by
its prologue at four to five microseconds and more blocks move it nowhere,
measured at 32 and 16 columns per block as well.

The launch-shape test took its row count from a constant that no longer
straddles the turn, so it takes it from the device instead.
perf(attention): pick the scorer's launch by blocks per SM, not by waves
6e5dfac 
The four-wave rule this replaces was fitted to two shapes and wrong on a third.
Sweeping rows at head dim 256 puts its turn at 1536 blocks with 4 blocks per SM,
which four waves calls at 1120, so the 8-head 256-dim shape went to the
eight-tile launch two row counts early: forcing each shape there, the eight-tile
one costs 1.31x at 40 rows and 1.16x at 48.

The occupancy is not what predicts the turn. Measured, the last block count the
single-tile shape wins and the first the eight-tile shape does:

  16 heads, head dim 128, 7 blocks/SM:   1536 then 2048
   4 heads, head dim 128, 7 blocks/SM:   2048 then 4096
   8 heads, head dim 256, 4 blocks/SM:   1536 then 2048

The first and third turn at the same block count with very different occupancy.
In waves their windows are (3.1, 4.2], (4.2, 8.4] and (5.5, 7.3] -- the first
two do not overlap at all, so no threshold in waves fits. Per SM they are
(21.9, 29.3], (29.3, 58.5] and (21.9, 29.3], which 24 splits. The occupancy
query is gone with the rule that needed it, and the block count is computed in
64 bits so a launch large enough to wrap cannot pick the wrong shape.

Four heads at 2048 blocks is the one point this gets wrong, by 1.09x. It and
the 2048 of the other two want opposite shapes, so no single threshold takes
all three.

Measured on SM80 only. The threshold decides which shape runs, never what it
computes, so elsewhere the worst case is a slower choice.

The test that pins the two shapes against each other took its row count from
the four-wave rule, so it takes it from this one instead, and the row-count
test above it no longer straddles a switch at all -- its name said it did.
bench(attention): time the sparse paged scorer
247e0aa 
Rows and columns are what a sparse-attention selector varies -- how many query
tokens a step scores at once, and how far back it looks -- so the shapes sweep
both, at the head counts either multiply width covers and at both head dims
that change the staging.

Replayed from a graph. The smallest shapes run in a few microseconds, the same
order as a launch, so timing them one launch at a time measures the launch as
much as the kernel.

The page table is shuffled so the gather chases pages rather than walking them
in order, and every eleventh entry is unmapped so the masked path is timed too.
Rows are spread over their request's sequence with the last one seeing all of
it: a row at position zero scores nothing.
fix(sparse): refuse a page that holds nothing, and format the headers
bacd2a3 
A cache with no pages is a shape the scorer handles: nothing to read, every
column masked. A cache whose pages hold no entries is not. The column is
divided by the page size to reach its page, so zero there is a divisor of zero,
and passing num_columns explicitly gets past the width the page table would
otherwise imply -- which reached the launch and died with an illegal access.
Rejected in the wrapper and in the binding, with a test.

The two headers this series touches were not clang-format clean: 18 places in
the scorer and 4 in cp_async.
fix(sparse): bound an index in its own width before narrowing it
394f98a 
The index tensors may be int64 and the kernel works in int32. The request and
the page ids were already safe: both are compared against their counts in
IdType, so anything an int32 could not hold is rejected before the cast. The
query position was not. Nothing bounded it from above, and a position of
exactly 2^32 narrows to zero -- a query that sees nothing, where it should have
been rejected as out of range.

All three now carry the bound explicitly so the next one cannot regress
quietly, and the tests cover 2^31, 2^32, INT64_MAX and a negative sentinel for
each of them. Removing the bounds fails the position at 2^32.
fix(sparse): compute the query end outside the width that overflows
1a461b1 
INT32_MAX is inside the range the position check accepts, and the visible count
is taken from position + 1, which in int32 is signed overflow. The end is now
formed in 64 bits before the divide.

The compression ratio carries an upper bound as well: it is narrowed to uint32
for the kernel, so 2^32 would arrive as zero and be divided by.

INT32_MAX joins the boundary tests as a value the kernel takes rather than one
it rejects -- what it exercises is the arithmetic after the cast. Reverting the
64-bit end fails it.
test(sparse): fail without the compression ratio's upper bound
b3c9e3c 
The bound was added without a case that needed it. A ratio of 2^32 narrows to
zero and becomes the divisor the kernel takes columns apart with; removing the
check fails this.
fix(sparse): check what the scorer's per-row indices are, and say wha…
4df8757 
…t failed

Four things the binding and the wrapper were letting through.

Each per-row index tensor was checked for contiguity and for its first extent,
which a `[rows, 2]` tensor satisfies. The kernel then read the flattened buffer
and scored against the wrong request, silently. All four carry a rank check now.

Every `cudaErrorInvalidValue` out of the launch was reported as an unsupported
head count, including the ones that are a rejected grid or shared-memory size.
The head count is checked on the host before dispatch, and whatever else comes
back is reported with its own message.

The capability cache keyed on `torch.device("cuda")` with no index, which
resolves through the current device but is a single key -- so on a host whose
GPUs differ, the first answer stood for all of them, which is what keying on
the device was for. The index is resolved before the cached call.

The benchmark asked for the default cold L2 while passing a closure the helper
cannot rotate tensors through, so it disabled itself with a warning and the
number read as cold. It asks for warm explicitly and the column says so.

Filter gen_sparse_scores_module() to SM80 and newer targets.

build_cuda_cflags() adds all configured architectures when the module provides no -gencode flags. Therefore, a mixed SM75/SM80 AOT build also compiles csrc/sparse_scores.cu for SM75. That source calls the SM80-only mma::mma_sync_m16n8k16_row_col_f16f16f32, so NVCC can reject the SM75 compilation. Pass architecture flags filtered to major versions 8 and newer.
